source_text:
Sic Caecilius et renidens (nam indignationis eius tumorem effusae orationis impetus relaxauerat): Ecquid ad haec, ait, audet Octauius, homo Plautinae prosapiae, ut Christianorum praecipuus, ita postremus philosophorum?
Parce, inquam, in eum plaudere: neque enim prius exultare te dignum est concinnitate sermonis, quam utrimque plenius fuerit peroratum, maxime cum non laudi, set ueritati disceptatio uestra nitatur.
etquamquam magnum in modum me subtili uarietate tua delectarit oratio, tamen altius moueor, non de praesenti actione, sed de toto genere disputandi, quod plerumque pro disserentium uiribus et eloquentiae potestate etiam perspicuae ueritatis condicio mutetur.
id accidere pernotum est auditorum facilitate, qui dum uerborum lenocinio a rerum intentionibus auocantur, sine dilectu adsentiuntur dictis omnibus nec a rectis falsa secernunt, nescientes inesse et in incredibili uerum et in uerisimili mendacium.
itaque quo saepius adseuerationibus credunt, eo frequentius a peritioribus arguuntur: sic adsidue temeritate decepti culpam iudicii sui transferunt ad incerti querellam, ut damnatis omnibus malint uniuersa suspendere quam de fallacibus iudicare.
igitur nobis prouidendum est, ne odio identidem sermonum omnium laboremus ita, ut in execrationem et odium hominum plerique simpliciores efferantur. nam incaute creduli circumueniuntur ab iis quos bonos putauerunt: mox errore consimili iam suspectis omnibus ut improbos metuunt etiam quos optimos sentire potuerunt.
nos proinde solliciti, quod utrimque omni in negotio disseratur et ex altera parte plerumque obscura sit ueritas, ex altero latere mira subtilitas, quae nonnumquam ubertate dicendi fidem confessae probationis imitetur, diligenter quantum potest singula ponderemus, ut argutias quidem laudare, ea uero quae recta sunt, eligere, probare, suscipere possimus.
thought_title: The judge calls for careful weighing, not applause
orientation: Marcus, the narrator and judge, responds after Caecilius has finished his opening speech against Christianity.
pass_a_gloss: Thus Caecilius, also smiling (for the force of his poured-out speech had relaxed the swelling of his indignation): Does Octavius dare anything against these things, he says, a man of Plautine stock, as he is the foremost of the Christians, so he is the last of the philosophers? Spare, I say, to applaud him: for it is not worthy for you to exult beforehand in the elegance of speech, before it has been pleaded more fully on both sides, especially since your debate strives not for praise, but for truth. And although your speech has delighted me greatly with its subtle variety, nevertheless I am moved more deeply, not about the present action, but about the whole kind of disputing, because generally according to the strength of the disputants and the power of eloquence even the condition of clear truth is changed. That this happens is very well known through the easiness of listeners, who, while they are called away from the intentions of the matters by the allurement of words, assent to all the sayings without discrimination, and do not separate false things from right things, not knowing that the true is present even in the unbelievable and a lie in the probable. And so the more often they believe assertions, the more frequently they are refuted by those more experienced: thus, continually deceived by rashness, they transfer the fault of their own judgment to a complaint about uncertainty, so that, having condemned all things, they prefer to suspend everything rather than to judge about deceptive things. Therefore we must take care, lest we labor again and again with hatred of all discourse, so that very many simpler people are carried away into cursing and hatred of men. For the incautiously credulous are surrounded by those whom they thought good: soon, by a similar error, now suspecting all men, they fear as wicked even those whom they could have perceived as best. We therefore, being anxious, because on both sides in every matter there is disputing, and on one side the truth is generally obscure, on the other side there is wonderful subtlety, which sometimes by richness of speaking imitates the credibility of confessed proof, let us weigh each thing carefully as much as possible, so that we may indeed praise clever arguments, but may be able to choose, approve, and take up those things which are right.

choices.why: Keeps the mocking reference to Octavius's family as descended from Plautus, implying low or comic origins, without smoothing it into a modern idiom.

choices.term: ut Christianorum praecipuus, ita postremus philosophorum
choices.english: as he is the foremost of the Christians, so he is the last of the philosophers
choices.why: Preserves the exact antithetical structure and the insulting force of 'last' as worst, not merely latest.
rejected: the best Christian but the worst philosopher
first among Christians, last among philosophers

choices.why: Renders the rhetorical polish Caecilius displayed, matching the judge's concern with style over substance.
Keeps the agricultural metaphor of abundance in speech, which the Latin uses to describe deceptive eloquence.
Literal rendering of the paradox: eloquence can imitate the trustworthiness of proof that has been openly admitted.

choices.term: argutias quidem laudare, ea uero quae recta sunt, eligere, probare, suscipere
choices.english: praise clever arguments, but choose, approve, and take up those things which are right
choices.why: Preserves the fourfold sequence of verbs and the contrast between praising style and accepting substance.
rejected: admire the cleverness but accept the truth
commend the wit and embrace what is correct

pass_b_english: So Caecilius smiled, for the flow of his speech had eased the swelling of his indignation, and said: "Does Octavius dare to answer this? He is a man of Plautus's family, and as he is the foremost of the Christians, so he is the last of the philosophers."

"Stop applauding him," I said. "You have no right to exult over the elegance of his speech before both sides have pleaded fully to the end, especially since your debate strives not for praise but for truth. And although your speech has delighted me greatly with its subtle variety, I am moved more deeply, not about the present case, but about the whole method of arguing, because the condition of even clear truth is often changed by the strength of the speakers and the power of their eloquence.

This happens, as everyone knows, through the indulgence of listeners, who are drawn away from the matters at hand by the allurement of words and assent to everything said without discrimination, not separating falsehoods from what is right, unaware that truth exists even in the incredible and falsehood in the plausible. So the more often they believe assertions, the more often they are refuted by those with greater skill. Thus, constantly deceived by their own rashness, they transfer the blame for their judgment to a complaint about uncertainty, so that, condemning everything, they prefer to suspend all matters rather than judge about deceptive things.

Therefore we must take care that we do not repeatedly suffer from hatred of all speech, so that many of the simpler sort are carried away into cursing and hating people. For the incautiously credulous are deceived by those whom they thought good; soon, by a similar error, they suspect everyone and fear as wicked even those whom they could have perceived as the best.

So let us be careful, since every matter is argued on both sides and on one side the truth is often obscure, while on the other there is remarkable subtlety, which sometimes imitates the credibility of confessed proof through richness of speaking. Let us weigh each point carefully, as much as we can, so that we may indeed praise clever arguments, but choose, approve, and take up those things which are right."

problems.quote: that we do not suffer from hatred of all speech in the same way
problems.source_quote: ne odio identidem sermonum omnium laboremus
problems.why: 'identidem' = 'repeatedly/again and again', not 'in the same way'; 'laboremus' = 'toil/suffer'.
problems.fix: that we do not repeatedly suffer from hatred of all speech
problems.ruling: ‘identidem’ = repeatedly, ‘laboremus’ = labor; English adds ‘in the same way’ and changes nuance.

edits.old: that we do not suffer from hatred of all speech in the same way
edits.new: that we do not repeatedly suffer from hatred of all speech

fixed: Changed 'in the same way' to 'repeatedly' to match 'identidem' in the source.

problems.quote: Minucius Felix (fl. c. 200) was a Roman lawyer and Christian apologist
problems.why: The narrator is named Marcus in the text but introduced only as 'the author' and 'Minucius Felix' in the intro, which may confuse readers about who is speaking.
problems.fix: Clarify that Marcus is Minucius Felix.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
problems.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.

problems.quote: He is a man of Plautus's family
problems.why: 'Plautus's family' is obscure; likely means a common or low-born family, not the comic poet.
problems.fix: Gloss or translate as 'of common stock' if that is the intended meaning.

edits.old: He is a man of Plautus's family
edits.new: He is a man of Plautine stock

fixed: The narrator is Marcus Minucius Felix, identified in the work brief as 'The narrator and author'; no edit needed to the English text.
The name 'Natalis' does not appear in this section; no edit needed.

The source reads 'homo Plautinae prosapiae', meaning 'a man of Plautine stock'. The English 'Plautus's family' is a reasonable rendering, but 'Plautine stock' is more precise and matches the source adjective. Edited.

last_rejected.why: English 'him' hides that narrator addresses Caecilius about Octavius; 'in eum plaudere' means 'applaud him' (Octavius), but context shows Marcus checks Caecilius.
last_rejected.ruling: in eum refers to Octavius; English 'him' correctly reflects that.

last_rejected.quote: suffer from hatred of all speech
last_rejected.why: 'laboremus' means 'toil' or 'be afflicted by,' but 'suffer from hatred' misrepresents syntax: 'odio...laboremus' = 'toil with hatred,' i.e., come to hate all discourse.
last_rejected.fix: we do not repeatedly grow to hate all discourse
last_rejected.ruling: laboremus with odio = toil/afflicted by hatred; translation conveys similar sense.

last_rejected.quote: carried away into cursing and hating people
last_rejected.source_quote: in execrationem et odium hominum plerique simpliciores efferantur
last_rejected.why: 'efferantur' = 'are carried away,' but 'execrationem' = 'execration/cursing' and 'odium hominum' = 'hatred of people' (objective genitive), not 'cursing and hating people.'
last_rejected.fix: many simpler folk are carried away into execration and hatred of people
last_rejected.ruling: efferantur in execrationem et odium hominum = carried into cursing and hatred of people.

last_rejected.why: 'confessae' = 'acknowledged/established,' not 'confessed'; 'fidem...imitetur' = 'imitates the trustworthiness of acknowledged proof.'
last_rejected.ruling: confessae can mean acknowledged; 'confessed proof' is acceptable rendering.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker transitions, made the opening question about Octavius more direct, and smoothed the sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: The pagan opponent is called Caecilius in most sections but addressed as Marcus in others, confusing the reader about identity.
notes.fix: Standardize the name to Caecilius or explain that Marcus is his praenomen.

notes.why: Octavius is suddenly called 'Januarius' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Januarius is an alternate name for Octavius.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

notes.why: 'Plautine stock' is obscure; reader may confuse with the playwright Plautus.
notes.fix: Note: possibly meaning low or common origin; clarify the reference.
